title: Issues with ai/algo trading
author: Maple-Research
selftext: What are some common or more so niche constant issues you guys come across when using AI for trading or backtesting your strategies or indicators?

comments.author: schoenheimeroliver
comments.body: One of the biggest issues is false confidence from a clean backtest. data leakage can be subtle, like fitting a scaler on the full dataset, using the current candle's close to enter at that same close, repeatedly tuning against the same test period, or excluding delisted assets. then there's the backtest to live a gap, spreads, fees, slippage, partial fills, latency, missing candles, time zone mismatches, and changing market conditions. a strategy trained during a low volatility trend can quickly lose its edge when the market becomes choppy. with AI generated code, the dangerous part is that it can run without errors while the trading logic is still wrong. i'd trust a modest result that survives walk forward testing and realistic costs more than a nearly perfect equity curve. are you seeing more issues with the data/model side or when moving from backtesting to paper or live trading?

replies.author: Maple-Research
replies.body: I offer a backtesting service for algo and ai trading strategys and I'm just wanting to build some conversations on if this is peoples main area of needing a tool in this type of industry. What would you value a tool that can offer the levels of proper testing that a tool such as quant connect offers but still being a no code easy to use tool that can save months of programming backtesting agents yourself? I've found backtesting to be the most consistent issue in this space and usually it's the lack of a easy to use tool.

replies.author: schoenheimeroliver
replies.body: That makes sense. for me, the biggest value wouldn't just be making backtesting no code. it would be building proper testing guardrails into the workflow. things like automatic in sample and out of sample separation, walki forward testing, realistic fess and slippage, leakage warnings, parameter sensitivity checks, and performance across dirfferent market conditions would make it genuinely useful. i'd also want every assumption to remain visible and exportable. otherwise, a no code tool could simply help people create misleading backtests faster. a robustness score or checklist may be more valuable than showing the highest possible return. who are you mainly building it for: traders with strategy ideas but no programming experience, or experienced quants who want a faster workflow?

replies.author: Maple-Research
replies.body:
All of the above has been considered. It is entirely possible to build a tool that considers slippage fees, OOS, parameter robustness etc in a no code way even running on genuine tick rate data. 

Given this is not something easy to make it's extremely expensive but we're looking to provide a easier way for people to get into algo trading and making sure there strategy is robust while also having a powerful enough tool that professionals can save extreme amounts of time not having to code.

 we also don't sell strategys at all to ensure a neutral testing environment environment as well and we have no benefit of fudging cherry picker reports like seller's do. 

It's also intended to be a highly valuable time saving tool for prosumers as well as potentially small hedge funds that haven't had the same time and experience to develop there own internal systems like Jane street and citadel.

comments.author: Consistent-Land-2389
comments.body: I have build a regime detection machine purely based on price action with only just 2 parameters and basically less prone to over fitting. It's actually build on btc daily and it's a 3 state machine with bull, bear and neutral. It also works out of sample in stocks and commodities and not so much on currencies. It can be used as a gate in algo trading and a context filter if you are a manual trader. I mean if you are looking to improve your game feel free to dm.

replies.author: Maple-Research
replies.body: I am not looking to improve my game just looking for people's issues in the space. I have my own software I sell that's solves these issues but I'm looking to expand into other people's common issues and wanting first hand knowledge.

comments.author: Good_Character_20
comments.body: The one that cost me most recently was a timestamp mismatch that never threw anything. Daily bars came stamped at the session open, the option chain rows were stamped at midnight, and the lookup joined the two on exact equality. Zero of 121 days matched. Every strategy came back with no entries. The runs completed cleanly and reported nothing kept, which is indistinguishable from an honest result about a ticker that simply had no edge. Finding it meant reading the code path rather than the output. That is the shape I watch for now. A crash is free information. The expensive failures are the ones that hand you a number you have no reason to doubt.

comments.author: Immediate-Owl-6916
comments.body:
A few that don't get talked about enough, in no particular order:

**Point-in-time data leakage in backtests.** A screener or indicator that uses fundamentals/data as they look *today* instead of as they looked *on the trade date* will quietly inflate every backtest result. Invisible in the equity curve, only shows up when live results don't match.

**Survivorship bias in the universe itself.** If your historical ticker universe is built from today's index constituents, you've silently excluded every company that got delisted, went bankrupt, or got acquired. Backtesting against "the S&P 500" using today's membership list isn't backtesting against history, it's backtesting against companies that already proved they'd survive.

**Vendor/platform risk that has nothing to do with your strategy.** Saw this play out in real time in another thread recently — someone's alert system got silently removed after their platform changed its broker integration, and a legit strategy took a loss because the infra failed at the wrong moment, not because the logic was wrong. Easy to blame the strategy when it's actually the plumbing.

**Multiple testing without correcting for it.** If you test 50 variations of an idea against the same historical data, you will find one that looks profitable by chance alone. That's not edge, that's the multiple comparisons problem. Doesn't mean testing variations is bad, just means the bar for "this one worked" needs to be a lot higher than "the backtest was green."

**Same-bar execution assumptions.** Filling a signal at the same candle's close it was generated on is a common accidental cheat — you're trading on information you technically didn't have yet at that exact price. Next-bar execution is more annoying to code and much closer to what you'd actually get filled at.

Curious what others run into, especially anything AI-specific rather than generic backtesting pitfalls.
